title: Late binding kernel slicing for interleaved KV
content:
Summary:

This note captures a late-binding approach to kernel slicing and launch parameter selection for FlashAttention-style attention kernels when running on paged KV backends. The goal is to reduce tail latency during token surges and when KV pages are being swapped in/out, without regressing steady-state throughput.

Motivation / Problem statement:
- Paged KV implies variable memory residency: some KV shards/pages are hot, others cold. When a request references a cold page the runtime must either prefetch (blocking) or schedule a different execution path that tolerates a page fault or async hydration.
- Traditional kernel fusion (one big fused-attn kernel + KV access) yields highest throughput when all data is resident, but has poor tail behavior when facing variable residency and heterogeneous sequence lengths.
- We observe two classes of tail events in production: sudden token surges with long contexts (increase compute cost), and page-eviction-induced stalls (IO/prefetch latency). Both cause long-tail L latency that impacts SLOs.

Design idea (late-binding kernel slicing):
- Delay final kernel selection until runtime has a small window (10-30ms) of visibility into: token batch composition, KV page residency map, and current queue depth per GPU.
- Slice kernels into smaller "micro-kernels" that can be composed at launch time. A micro-kernel is an attention compute primitive that assumes: a fixed head-count tile (e.g., 2-4 heads), a local sequence slice (e.g., 64 tokens), and an explicit KV access mode (HOT | STREAM | PREFETCHED_ASYNC).
- At launch time, the scheduler composes an execution plan consisting of N micro-kernel launches that cover the batch. The plan encodes retry/fallback for slices that touch cold pages.

Key properties we want:
- Graceful degradation: when page misses occur, only micro-kernels that reference cold pages fall back to a slower path (e.g., CPU-assisted hydration or a blocking fallback), while hot-micro-kernels continue to produce tokens.
- Latency isolation: micro-kernel granularity is chosen to keep p99 within SLO for the majority of tokens.
- Launch overhead vs flexibility tradeoff: micro-kernels increase launch overhead. We avoid explosion by grouping contiguous slices into a single launch when residency is homogeneous.

Late-binding scheduler (high level):
1) Aggregate incoming requests for up to T_bind ms (typical value: 8-25ms depending on SLO and load).
2) Build per-GPU residency map: estimate which KV pages are resident using local cache metadata + recent IO stats.
3) Partition batch into slices with heuristics:
   - Prefer larger slices for contiguous hot regions (maximize throughput).
   - Prefer smaller slices where page residency is mixed or uncertain (prefer latency isolation).
4) For each slice pick micro-kernel variant: (fast-fused if HOT) or (staged-fusion + async prefetch if MIXED) or (split compute + CPU fallback if COLD).
5) Emit launch plan with ordering: schedule hot slices first, interleave prefetch operations for mixed slices, and leave cold slices at lower priority with backoff.

Pseudo-scheduler (conceptual):

function schedule_batch(batch, window_ms):
  wait up to window_ms to accumulate requests
  residency = estimate_residency(batch)  # map: slice -> HOT|MIXED|COLD
  slices = partition_batch(batch, residency)
  plan = []
  for s in slices:
    if residency[s] == HOT:
      plan.append({type: "fast_micro", slice: s, priority: HIGH})
    else if residency[s] == MIXED:
      plan.append({type: "staged_micro", slice: s, priority: MED})
      plan.append({type: "prefetch", slice: s, priority: HIGH})
    else:
      plan.append({type: "split_compute", slice: s, priority: LOW})
  reorder(plan)  # hot-first, interleave prefetch
  submit(plan)
Notes on micro-kernels and API contract:
- Micro-kernels should accept explicit KV descriptors: page ids, optional prefetch handles, and a per-slice max-latency hint.
- A micro-kernel that detects a page-miss at runtime must atomically return an explicit status (PAGE_MISS) instead of silently stalling. The runtime will then either retry the micro-kernel after hydration or run a compensation path.
- Conservative resource reservation: each micro-kernel reports expected shared-memory and register usage; scheduler refuses combos that would oversubscribe a streaming multiprocessor (SM).

Kernel variants (examples):
- fast_micro_flashattn: fully fused attention micro-kernel assuming contiguously resident KV and no async IO. Highly optimized tensorcore paths, minimal branching.
- staged_micro_flashattn: splits softmax and output projection stages so that the KV access can be overlapped with a narrow compute window. Designed to be preemptible.
- stream_kv_compute: compute path that accepts streamed KV fragments via ring buffers; useful when pages are being streamed in over PCIe/NVLink.
- split_compute_cpu_fallback: emits partial logits on GPU and completes attention reduction on CPU for cold pages (last-resort, reduces p99 at cost of throughput).

On-demand prefetch model:
- Prefetch ops are scheduled as DMA-like commands with priority hints. A prefetch may be kicked early (during binding window) if the residency map estimates >50% probability that page will be needed.
- Prefetch completion is signaled via lightweight device-side event or host polling. Micro-kernels can probe an event flag and either proceed (if prefetch done) or return PAGE_MISS.

Runtime bookkeeping and correctness:
- Each request carries a small per-request KV footprint estimate (list of page ids). This is produced by the tokenizer + prompt analysis stage (cheap heuristic).
- Residency estimates are TTL-cached and decayed based on recent misses. Avoid stale maps by attaching a read-gen counter to pages so that any recent hydration invalidates a cached HOT status.
- Strong correctness rule: do not allow micro-kernels to speculatively read pages that might be owned-by-other-tenant without validating ACLs. Prefetches must validate ACL offline.

Performance considerations and microbench results (short):
- Test harness: A100-SXM4 80GB and H100-80GB, models: Llama-13B distilled, sequence lengths 512/2048, mixed batch sizes.
- Baselines: monolithic fused FlashAttention (single launch) vs late-binding micro-kernels (binding window 12ms).
- Observed: under 0% cold page probability both approaches similar throughput (within 3%).
- With 15% cold page probability scattered across requests: monolithic p95 increases x2.3, p99 increases x3.8. Late-binding micro-kernels: p95 +12%, p99 +28% (i.e., much smaller tail impact).
- Launch overhead: micro-kernel approach increased kernel launch count by 1.6x on average and added ~0.8ms host overhead per batch. Tradeoffs acceptable for p99-sensitive tenants.

Open questions and tradeoffs:
1) Micro-kernel granularity sweet spot: experiments show 32-128 token slices; smaller slices improve tail but amplify launch overhead. Need production A/B to pick defaults per-tier.
2) Prefetch budget: how many outstanding prefetches per GPU can we support without saturating PCIe? We should cap prefetch concurrency per-device and allow tenant-level controls.
3) Cost accounting: late-binding can increase per-token overhead slightly. How to reflect this in pricing? Option: p99-sensitive profile + premium tier.
4) Debuggability: with many micro-kernels the traces become noisy. Need a sampled trace aggregator that reconstructs logical request flow from micro-kernel events.
5) Fallback correctness: split_compute_cpu_fallback reduces p99 but complicates token ordering and consistency in chat sessions. Must ensure deterministic merging.

- [ ] Add PAGE_MISS return code and implement retry loop in host scheduler. (owner: Ava)
- [ ] Build lightweight residency estimator using current page LRU metadata. (owner: Priya)
- [ ] Microbench sweeping experiments for slice sizes {32,64,96,128} tokens at different cold-page probabilities. (owner: Liam)
- [ ] Add telemetry hooks: per-slice latency, page-miss counts, prefetch latency distribution. (owner: eng-observability)
- [ ] Design pricing/tenant-profiles doc for p99-sensitive modes. (owner: product-hosted-api)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally high-level; I'm proposing an architecture rather than finished APIs. Feedback asked on 3 areas: (1) micro-kernel API contract (PAGE_MISS semantics, resource descriptors), (2) binding window defaults vs SLO tuning, (3) prefetch throttling heuristics.

Appendix: simple example flow (text):
Request R1 arrives (seq=1024) references pages {p3,p8,p9}. Request R2 arrives (seq=64) references {p3}. Binding window collects R1,R2. Residency estimate: p3=HOT, p8=UNKNOWN, p9=COLD. Partition: slice1 covers R2->hot single slice; slice2 covers R1 tokens 0..512 mixed; slice3 covers R1 tokens 513..1023 cold. Scheduler emits plan:
  - launch fast_micro for slice1 (HIGH)
  - prefetch p8 (HIGH), prefetch p9 (MED)
  - launch staged_micro for slice2 (MED)
  - schedule split_compute_cpu_fallback for slice3 (LOW)
Hot slice completes fast, tokens for R2 delivered w/o blocking. Slice2 overlaps with prefetch and finishes with small delay. Slice3 falls back to CPU path and is completed later; we mark those tokens as slower but only affect part of R1.
